request: add an AI Engineer folder with RAG in detail: how it works, types of RAG and use cases
title: When RAG breaks, and how to fix it

steps.caption: The interviewer sets the problem.

problem.statement: Your RAG assistant is live and real users are finding problems. Find what breaks, why, and the fix for each one.
example: Another company’s numbers show up in an answer
Confident answers that are not in the documents
constraints: Answers must stay grounded in your documents
Fixes should not slow every question much
You must be able to prove each fix helped
problem.followUp: How would you prove a fix actually improved things?

steps.caption: What the interviewer is really asking.

plain.asking: Fix a RAG system *one failure at a time*: work out whether *finding* or *writing* failed, apply the matching fix, then measure.
points: *You get:* an assistant that is right most of the time.
*You do:* find each failure’s cause and fix only that part.
*The catch:* a fix in one place can hurt another, so measure.

steps.caption: A chunk can lose its context. “Revenue grew 3% over the last quarter” doesn’t say *whose* revenue. Ask about ACME, get another company’s chunk.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

steps.eyebrow: Fix: add context to each chunk
steps.caption: Before embedding, have an AI prepend a short note to every chunk: “From ACME’s Q2 report: revenue grew 3%…”. Anthropic calls this *contextual retrieval*.

steps.caption: Vectors are fuzzy. Search “error E-4012” and they find pages about errors *in general*. An exact code has little “meaning”, so the one page that names it is missed.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

steps.caption: Add a classic *keyword index* (BM25) beside the vector index. Keywords catch exact codes and names; vectors catch meaning. Run both, then merge the lists.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

items.label: KEYWORD INDEX
items.note: A classic search index (BM25) that matches exact words, codes and names.

items.label: PROMPT
items.note: Question + the retrieved chunks + the rules for answering.

steps.caption: Your turn.

check.question: Searching “error E-4012” returns pages about errors in general. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Add keyword (BM25) search next to vector search
Switch to a bigger AI model
check.explain: The problem is *retrieval*, not the AI. Keyword search matches the exact code, and merging with vector results keeps both strengths.

labels.text: “I couldn’t find that in the documents.”

steps.caption: Your turn.

check.question: A user asks about something that is not in your documents. What should the assistant do?
options: Say it couldn’t find it in the documents
Answer from its general knowledge anyway
Return the nearest chunk as the answer
check.explain: A trustworthy RAG assistant knows the limits of its sources. “I don’t know” beats a confident wrong answer.

steps.caption: Measure the two halves *separately*. First retrieval: for test questions with known answers, was the right chunk in the top k? That score is called *recall@k*.

steps.caption: Fixes stack. In Anthropic’s published test, “right chunk missing from the top 20” fell from 5.7% to 1.9% as context, keywords and reranking were added.

steps.caption: Not every problem needs RAG. Pick by the shape of your data and what you need from the AI:

items.text: Put it all in the prompt

labels.text: IF EVERYTHING FITS IN ONE PROMPT
IF DATA IS BIG OR CHANGES OFTEN
IF YOU NEED A STYLE, NOT FACTS
teaches behaviour · bad at fresh facts

steps.caption: The big idea: *each RAG fix targets one failure*: context for lost meaning, keywords for exact terms, reranking for noise, rules for honesty. Measure, then fix.
